script.title: A Spacecraft Has Mapped Almost Every Metre of the Moon
script.description: Since 2009, NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has mapped the Moon's surface in precise detail. From ancient impact basins to silent astronaut footprints, these images reveal a world preserved in time.

shots.narration: Since 2009, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has circled the Moon, photographing almost every square metre.
The Moon is 3,474 kilometres wide and orbits 384,400 kilometres away from Earth.
This distant world is constantly changing position, drifting outward by 3.8 centimetres every year.
The South Pole-Aitken basin spans 2,500 kilometres across and drops 8 kilometres deep.
Near the lunar poles, deep craters have not seen sunlight in billions of years.
Their frozen floors drop colder than minus 230 °C and hold ancient water ice.
Tycho crater measures 86 kilometres wide, featuring a central peak about 2 kilometres tall.
Without wind or rain, footprints left behind by astronauts will last for millions of years.
Detailed mapping preserves the exact landscape where human footsteps remain preserved in history.
